# Introduction

Quarto turns a plain-text source into many outputs. One document can become a
web page, a PDF typeset with LaTeX or Typst, or a Word file, while the
analysis that produces its numbers lives right next to the prose.

The workflow is short:

1. Write text and code in a `.qmd` file
2. Choose one or more output formats in the front matter
3. Render, and re-render whenever the data changes

> Code runs where the prose lives, so results never drift out of date.

# Results

@tbl-penguins summarises the Palmer penguins data set. Values are means per
species.

| Species   | Count | Bill (mm) | Mass (g) |
|-----------|------:|----------:|---------:|
| Adelie    |   152 |      38.8 |    3,701 |
| Chinstrap |    68 |      48.8 |    3,733 |
| Gentoo    |   124 |      47.5 |    5,076 |

: Penguin measurements by species {#tbl-penguins}

The sample mean of $n$ observations is

$$
\bar{x} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i .
$$ {#eq-mean}

::: {.callout-note}
## Callouts

Callouts come in five flavours: note, tip, important, caution and warning.
:::

## Computation

Code chunks run at render time. This listing is shown, not executed:

```python
import seaborn as sns

df = sns.load_dataset("penguins")
df.groupby("species").bill_length_mm.mean().round(1)
```

# Discussion

Plain text sources are friendly to version control, review and
collaboration. Because every number in @tbl-penguins and every result derived
from @eq-mean is computed during rendering, the report stays correct as the
data evolves. Cross-references, citations and figure numbering are handled
for every output format alike.
